name: Estonian
sources: Asu, Eva Liina; Teras, Pire (2009). Estonian. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 39(3): 367-372.
Lehiste, Ilse (1960). Segmental and syllabic quantity in Estonian. American Studies in Uralic Linguistics 1: 21-82. Bloomington: Indiana University.
Lehiste, Ilse (1997). Search for phonetic correlates in Estonian prosody. In Lehiste, Ilse & Ross, Jaan (eds.), Estonian Prosody: Papers from a Symposium. Tallinn: Institute of Estonian Language.
Lippus, Pärtel; Asu, Eva Liina; Teras, Pire; Tuisk, Tuuli (2013). Quantity-related variation of duration, pitch and vowel quality in spontaneous Estonian. Journal of Phonetics 41(1): 17-28.
Meister, Einar; Meister, Lya (2019). Production of Estonian vowels by Finnish speakers. Eesti ja soome-ugri keeleteaduse ajakiri / Journal of Estonian and Finno-Ugric Linguistics 10(1): 129-143.

Leppik, Katrin; Lippus, Pärtel; Asu, Eva Liina (2019). The production of Estonian vowels in three quantity degrees by Spanish L1 speakers. Proceedings of the 19th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences, Melbourne.
Asu, Eva Liina (2004). The Phonetics and Phonology of Estonian Intonation. PhD dissertation, University of Cambridge.

Grabe, Esther; Low, Ee Ling (2002). Durational variability in speech and the Rhythm Class Hypothesis. In Gussenhoven, Carlos & Warner, Natasha (eds.), Laboratory Phonology 7. Mouton de Gruyter, 515-546.
Lehtonen, Jaakko (1970). Aspects of Quantity in Standard Finnish. Studia Philologica Jyväskyläensia VI. University of Jyväskylä. (quotes earlier Estonian duration ratios)

vowel_formants.speaker: adult male (mean of 7 native speakers), first-syllable stressed vowels in read sentences, the three quantity degrees pooled

contrasts: three degrees of quantity: short (Q1), long (Q2) and overlong (Q3), a property of the stressed two-syllable foot carried by the vowel, the following consonant or both (sada, saada, saada; lina, linna, linna)
nine vowel qualities, including the back unrounded /ɤ/ (written õ) and the front rounded /y ø/
plain versus palatalised alveolars: /t s n l/ against /tʲ sʲ nʲ lʲ/ (palk 'wages' against palk 'log')
stops differ in length, not voicing: short (written b d g), long (p t k) and overlong (pp tt kk), all voiceless
a large set of diphthongs (36 in stressed syllables according to Asu & Teras 2009)
allophony: stops are voiceless unaspirated; the short ones (written b d g) can be partly or fully voiced between voiced sounds
palatalisation is heard mainly as an i-like transition before the consonant (pre-palatalisation); it occurs before /i/ and /j/ and in words where a following i has been lost
/ɤ/ varies by speaker between close-mid back [ɤ], close back [ɯ] and mid central [ɘ]
short (Q1) vowels are more central in quality than long and overlong ones
the second-syllable vowel is longest (half-long) after a Q1 first syllable and shortest after a Q3 first syllable
word-initial /h/ is often dropped in casual speech
/v/ has weak friction and is often an approximant
phonotactics: no vowel harmony in the standard language; /o ɤ æ ø y/ are largely confined to first syllables, later syllables of native words have /ɑ e i u/
long vowels and diphthongs occur in syllables with primary or secondary stress
initial consonant clusters occur mainly in loanwords
the spelling shows Q2 against Q3 only for stops (p t k against pp tt kk); for vowels and other consonants both are written double

stress.rule: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of native words (a few words such as aitäh and many loanwords are stressed later); secondary stress falls on odd-numbered syllables or on particular suffixes.
stress.cues: the duration ratio of the stressed syllable to the following one and the alignment of the F0 peak; intensity plays little part, and there is no vowel reduction beyond the smaller vowel set of non-initial syllables

rhythm.vowel_reduction: none or slight; unstressed syllables keep clear vowels
rhythm.notes: Timing is organised by the two-syllable foot, whose internal duration ratio signals the quantity degree.

length.notes: Quantity is a foot-level pattern. The typical ratio of first (stressed) to second syllable duration is 2:3 in Q1, 3:2 in Q2 and 2:1 in Q3 (Lehiste 1960, 1997; Asu & Teras 2009); in spontaneous speech Lippus et al. (2013) report about 0.8 for Q1, 1.8 to 2.3 for Q2 and 2.6 to 3.4 for Q3. Mean first-syllable vowel durations in read sentences are 73 ms (Q1), 130 ms (Q2) and 158 ms (Q3) (Leppik, Lippus & Asu 2019). An older laboratory figure for the vowels alone is 1 : 2.19 : 3.53 (Liiv 1961, quoted by Lehtonen 1970). Q3 also differs from Q2 in pitch: the fall comes early within the first syllable in Q3, but at the end of the first syllable in Q1 and Q2.

intonation.declarative: a series of falling accents (H*+L) on stressed first syllables, each lower than the one before, ending low
intonation.yes_no_question: usually marked by the initial particle kas or by word order and spoken with a falling contour, often from a higher start; a final rise is possible but uncommon
intonation.wh_question: high accent on the initial question word, then falling
intonation.continuation: level pitch or a slight rise at the end of a non-final phrase
intonation.accent_shape: H*+L: high on the stressed syllable followed by a fall, which starts earlier in Q3 words than in Q1 and Q2 words

tone.notes: No lexical tone, but the timing of the F0 fall is a secondary cue to the difference between Q2 and Q3.

problems: Q2 and Q3 are told apart only where the spelling or a few rules allow it (pp, tt, kk; a long vowel in a monosyllable; k, p, t after a long vowel or sonorant); since vowels and most consonants are written alike in Q2 and Q3 (linna, kooli, saada), most Q3 words are spoken as Q2
no pitch difference between Q2 and Q3: the early fall of Q3 is not produced
õ has a central rounded quality, printed [ɵ], instead of back unrounded [ɤ]

palatalisation is guessed from the spelling and overapplied: l, n, s, t before i or j become full palatals such as [ʎ] (tuli is given as [tuʎɪ]), and nearly every word-final ll, nn, ss, tt after a vowel is palatalised
short b, d, g between vowels are fully voiced stops; Estonian has short voiceless stops with at most partial voicing

the half-long second-syllable vowel of Q1 words is produced only in words that begin with one consonant or none followed by vowel, single consonant, vowel, and it is given a laxer quality (phonemes A1, E1, I1, O1, U1; final i is printed [ɪ])
questions get a rising tune (intonation group 3), whereas Estonian questions usually fall
good: long vowels are separate phonemes with about twice the length of short ones, and overlong vowels are produced in monosyllables
palatalised consonants are preceded by a short i-glide, which matches the pre-palatalisation described in the literature
word-initial b, d, g are voiceless
geminates and n before k, g as [ŋ]

notes: The diphthong list gives the common native ones. The formant values pool the three quantity degrees; Q1 vowels are more central and Q2 and Q3 vowels more peripheral than these means.
